title: His own or someone else's
goal: Tell *sin* apart from *hans* and *hennes* — a distinction English doesn't make, and one that can change the meaning of a sentence completely — while learning all the object pronouns.
bekal: use *sin/si/sitt/sine* only when the owner is the subject of that same sentence
recognize when *hans* and *hennes* are actually the right choice
wave: Go back over **Unit 8** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Test just one thing — what's the difference between *må ikke* and *trenger ikke*?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — En liten misforståelse
dialogs.intro: Sunday afternoon. Lars can be heard on the phone in the next room, and Budi has just asked something that makes Ingrid put down her cup.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Lars ringer til moren sin hver søndag.
lines.id: Lars calls his mother every Sunday.
lines.literal: Lars rings to the-mother his-own every Sunday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Til moren hans? Hvem sin mor?
lines.literal: to the-mother his? who his mother?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Nei — **sin**. «Moren hans» ville betydd en annen manns mor.
lines.id: No — *sin*. *Moren hans* would mean another man's mother.
lines.literal: no — his-own. "the-mother his" would meant an other man's mother.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Nettopp. Han tar bilen sin — sin egen bil. Han tar bilen hans — en annens bil.
lines.id: Exactly. *Han tar bilen sin* — his own car. *Han tar bilen hans* — someone else's car.
lines.literal: exactly. he takes the-car his-own — his-own own car. he takes the-car his — an other's car.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det finnes ikke noe slikt på indonesisk. Vi sier bare «mobilnya».
lines.id: There's nothing like that in Indonesian. We just say *mobilnya*.
lines.literal: it exists not anything such in Indonesian. we say just "car-his".

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da må du høre godt etter. Feilen kan bli pinlig.
lines.id: Then you'll have to listen carefully. The mistake can get embarrassing.
lines.literal: then must you hear well after. the-mistake can become embarrassing.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: En student sa til læreren: «Jeg liker kona hans.» Han mente si egen.
lines.id: A student said to the teacher: "I like his wife." He meant his own.
lines.literal: a student said to the-teacher: "I like the-wife his." he meant his-own own.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Han så på ham lenge. Så lo han. Vi husker det ennå.
lines.id: He looked at him for a long time. Then he laughed. We still remember it.
lines.literal: he looked at him long. then laughed he. we remember it still.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Fra nå av sier jeg bare «moren til Lars».
lines.id: From now on I'll just say *moren til Lars*.
lines.literal: from now off say I just "the-mother to Lars".

notes: **This is a distinction English simply doesn't have.** English *his* does two jobs at once: "Lars calls his mother" can mean his own mother or another man's mother. Norwegian forces you to choose, and the choice changes who is meant.

**The rule is one sentence long: use *sin* when the owner is the subject of that same sentence.** *Han tar bilen **sin*** — Lars's own car. *Han tar bilen **hans*** — the car of some other man we're talking about.

**As a result, *sin* can never be part of the subject.** *Sin bil er rød* is impossible — there's no earlier subject for it to refer to. The right form is *Bilen hans er rød*. A useful quick test: if the possessive sits inside the subject of the sentence, it can't be *sin*.

**Sin is only for the third person.** With *jeg* and *du* there's no problem, because *min* and *din* already clearly point to yourself. So you only need to watch out when the subject is *han*, *hun*, *de* or a person's name.

**Fortell meg** — notice *meg*, not *jeg*. Norwegian pronouns change form when they're the object of an action, exactly like English (*I* → *me*). So this pattern will feel familiar; you just need the new words.

**Han så på ham** uses two different pronouns for two different people — *han* is the subject, *ham* the object, like *he* and *him*. In everyday speech many Norwegians use *han* for both, and that's accepted; *ham* remains the standard written form.

grammars.title: Pronouns: subject and object forms
body: You've been using the first column since Unit 1. The second column is the new one — it's used when the pronoun is the **object** of an action, or stands after a preposition.
after: Three rows don't change at all: *den*, *det*, *dere*. The ones to learn are just these: **meg, deg, ham, henne, oss, dem**.
*Meg* is pronounced **mai** and *deg* **dai** — the *g* turns into *i*, just as in *jeg* → **yai**. These three words travel together; learn their sounds at the same time.
After a preposition it's always the object form: *til meg*, *med deg*, *hos henne*, *fra dem*. No exceptions — just as in English (*to me*, *with her*).

grammars.title: Sin versus hans/hennes
body: Read this table row by row and watch how the meaning shifts from one person to another.

head: Norsk
Whose is it?
English
rows: his car (the car is the subject)

after: The last row shows an exception that isn't really one: there *bilen* is the **subject** of the sentence, so *sin* can't be used.

*Sin* agrees with the gender of the thing owned, not the owner: *bilen sin*, *boka si*, *huset sitt*, *barna sine*. Whether the owner is a man or a woman makes no difference at all — which is actually a simplification compared with *his/her*.
⚠️ The most common mistake: using *sin* when the owner is first or second person. *Jeg tar bilen sin* is wrong — it has to be *bilen min*. *Sin* lives only in the world of the third person.

grammars.title: The three-step test
body: If you're unsure between *sin* and *hans/hennes*, run through these three questions in order. It never fails.

head: Step
Question
If the answer is
rows: Is the subject third person (*han/hun/de*/a name)?
Does the thing belong to **the subject of this sentence**?
Is the possessive itself part of the **subject**?

after: In practice, step 1 already filters out most of the sentences you make every day. The only ones left to check are sentences telling a story about other people.
The safe route if you're really stuck mid-conversation: use the *til* pattern — *moren til Lars*, *bilen til Ingrid*. It always makes the owner clear and is never wrong.

sections.title: Eye training: two sentences, two people

blocks.text: Read each pair aloud and say out loud who the owner is. This drill looks trivial, and it's exactly the one that gets the rule in place fastest.

head: With sin
With hans/hennes/deres
The difference
rows: his own car / someone else's car
her own book / someone else's book
their own food / other people's food
his own key / someone else's key
her own sister / someone else's sister
their own teacher / other people's teacher

blocks.text: The right-hand column almost always feels odd when nobody else is being talked about — and that's the giveaway. If you use *hans* with no other "he" around, a Norwegian will stop and ask *hvem sin?* (whose?)
Object pronouns turn up most often with the following verbs. Practice them together.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Take ten sentences from the table above and swap the object each time: *meg, deg, ham, henne, oss, dere, dem*. Say them all out loud.
Then say three things about a friend using *sin*, and three things about some other person using *hans* or *hennes*.

If you're still unsure after five minutes, don't panic — even young native speakers sometimes get it wrong, and the mistake rarely gets in the way of understanding. What matters is that you **know the difference exists**.
